messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Miriam Calloway is a 73-year-old widowed painter who presented for her initial assessment carrying a canvas tote bag and speaking carefully, as though she had rehearsed what she was willing to say. She lives alone in a small house on the outskirts of a mid-sized Ohio town, where she has kept a studio for decades. She was referred by her primary care physician after her sleep difficulties and what she described as "losing herself" had persisted for over a year following a gas explosion at a community arts centre she had attended regularly. The blast, caused by a ruptured industrial line that building management had been warned about months earlier, killed two people and injured several others. Miriam was in a back hallway when the explosion occurred. She was thrown against a wall and lay on the concrete floor in the dark, unable to move, surrounded by the acrid smell of gas and burning material, while a man nearby wept loudly and uncontrollably. She was eventually pulled out by emergency responders, but for what she described as an indeterminate stretch of time, she was certain she was going to die there, alone, on a cold floor, in a building that should have been safe.

In the weeks that followed, Miriam found that certain things returned her immediately to the hallway. The smell of alcohol-based solvents — unavoidable in her own studio — would stop her at the door, her chest tightening, her body bracing as though the floor might give way. When someone cried near her, even on television, she would feel her pulse spike and her attention narrow. Physical touch, even gentle contact from her daughter during visits, could send a wave of alarm through her that she could not explain and could not stop. These triggers did not simply unsettle her — they pulled her directly into memory, vivid and unmoving, as though she were looking at a series of photographs she had not consented to keep: the angle of the hallway ceiling, the particular darkness, her own hand flat against the concrete. With those images came a bodily certainty that her limbs were pressed against the floor again, her back against the wall, her body arranged in the posture of someone waiting to die. And with the memories came guilt — a persistent, irrational conviction that she had failed to warn others, that she had not acted, that she had simply lain there.

That guilt had hardened, over months, into something more structural. Miriam had come to believe that the world did not operate the way she had spent seventy-three years assuming it did — that institutions could not be trusted, that safety was a story people told themselves, that she herself was somehow changed in a way that could not be undone. She was not sure, she said quietly, that her life was worth living anymore. She no longer believed she would feel ordinary emotions again; what she experienced instead was a kind of flatness interrupted by alarm. These appraisals had a way of sharpening her vigilance — she lay awake at night listening for sounds at the doors and windows, certain that her sense of threat was now permanently recalibrated. She was frequently irritable with the few people she saw, and her daughter had begun visiting less often, a loss Miriam registered with a grief she could not fully access. The negative beliefs also seemed to lower her threshold for being triggered — a world perceived as fundamentally unsafe meant that the smell of solvent or the sound of crying carried a weight they might not otherwise have borne. And when memories surfaced, they did not soften her appraisals but confirmed them, cycling back into the conviction that she was permanently altered and permanently at risk, which in turn kept her body in a state of readiness that made sleep almost impossible.

To manage all of this, Miriam had stopped watching the news entirely and kept her television tuned only to gardening programmes. She worked to keep her mind occupied at all hours — listening to audiobooks while she painted, filling silence aggressively. She tried hard not to think about the explosion, pushing images away the moment they surfaced. Her studio output, once prolific, had slowed considerably; she could rarely tolerate the smell of the solvents long enough to work for more than an hour.

What finally brought her in was her daughter's tearful plea during a recent visit — the crying itself had triggered an episode, and Miriam had asked her to leave. She arrived at the clinic hoping, she said, to feel like herself again, and most afraid that she no longer knew who that was.
